body:
Location and settlement arrangement

Lothal is an important Harappan settlement in Gujarat, situated near the Bhogavo River, a tributary of the Sabarmati, in the region connected with the Gulf of Khambhat. Its geographical position helped connect inland production with routes towards the coast.

The settlement had an upper and lower town within a fortified perimeter. The elevated upper area, conventionally called the citadel, stood on a substantial mud-brick platform. Unlike the citadel at Mohenjodaro, it was not enclosed by an additional separate fortification wall. Streets, drains and bathing platforms reflect the same concern for planned construction visible at other Harappan settlements.

The large basin and its interpretation

The most widely recognised architectural feature at Lothal is a large rectangular brick-lined basin adjoining the settlement. Excavators interpreted it as a dockyard or tidal basin that could receive boats, with arrangements identified as an inlet and outlet for controlling water. This interpretation is supported by the site's coastal connections and associated evidence of trade.

The dockyard identification, however, is an archaeological interpretation. Although frequently presented in textbooks as a major achievement of Harappan maritime engineering, its precise operation and function have also been debated. It is more accurate to describe the structure as a large basin commonly interpreted as a dockyard than to treat every aspect of its ancient use as conclusively demonstrated.

Workshops, storage and exchange

Lothal was also a centre of craft production. Excavations yielded evidence associated with bead-making, including raw material, unfinished beads, tools and completed products. Semi-precious stones were important materials in Harappan bead manufacture.

A substantial structure at Lothal has been interpreted as a warehouse. Seals and sealings recovered from the site support the importance of storing and identifying goods. A sealing is the impression made when a seal is pressed onto a material such as wet clay. Such impressions could be used to mark or secure packages.

These finds do not merely indicate the presence of traders. Together, the workshops, storage arrangements, seals and proposed harbour basin help explain why Lothal is regarded as an important centre in Harappan exchange networks.

Other sites and their distinguishing features

SitePresent locationArchitectural association
MohenjodaroPakistanGreat Bath, citadel, extensive drains
DholaviraGujaratStone fortifications and reservoirs
LothalGujaratLarge proposed dockyard basin and workshops
KalibanganRajasthanFortified settlement; structures interpreted as fire altars

The identification of some Kalibangan structures as fire altars is based on archaeological interpretation. Their presence does not establish that all Harappan cities shared an identical religious practice.

Conservation and heritage status

Harappan buildings survive as incomplete archaeological remains. Their preservation requires careful attention to fragile brickwork, site drainage, exposure to weather and the context of excavated structures. Replacing an ancient structure with an attractive modern reconstruction would not automatically preserve its historical evidence.

As of 23 November 2026, Lothal appears on India's UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List under the title Archaeological Remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal. The proposal was submitted on 15 April 2014. Tentative List status is not the same as inscription on the World Heritage List.

Prelims focus

  • Lothal is in Gujarat, near the Bhogavo River and Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Its large rectangular basin is commonly identified as a dockyard.
  • Lothal provides evidence of bead manufacture, seals and a proposed warehouse.
  • Its raised citadel was not separately walled.
  • Lothal is on the UNESCO Tentative List, with a submission date of 15 April 2014.
  • Trap: Dholavira is inscribed on the World Heritage List; Lothal's Tentative List entry is not an inscription.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 6–11; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, pp. 39–40; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological Remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal, Tentative List entry 5918, Description and Submission details, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The large basin at Lothal and the features underlying its dockyard interpretation.

title: Lothal: Gujarat's Harappan Trade Centre and the Question of the Dockyard

body:
Meaning and religious function

A stupa is a mound-like monument associated especially with Buddhism. Early stupas were often constructed to enshrine relics, such as bodily remains of the Buddha or revered monks, or objects associated with them. Such relics were placed within a mound or a specially prepared central deposit. The monument then became a focus of reverence.

The tradition of building memorial mounds is older than Buddhism, but stupas acquired particular importance as Buddhist sacred monuments. Buddhist texts, including the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, connect reverence for the Buddha's remains with the erection of stupas. The Ashokavadana describes Ashoka's distribution of relics and patronage of stupas. These are textual traditions about their development, while surviving monuments and inscriptions provide material evidence.

The principal parts of a stupa

Architectural termMeaningPosition or function
AndaHemispherical moundMain domed mass of the stupa
MedhiRaised drum or platformSupports the dome; may provide an elevated path
HarmikaSmall square railing-like structureAbove the dome
YashtiVertical mastRises above the harmika
ChhatraUmbrella-shaped elementSurmounts the mast
VedikaEnclosing railingDefines the sacred enclosure
ToranaMonumental gatewayMarks an entrance through the railing
PradakshinapathaCircumambulatory pathAllows movement around the monument

The basic form developed over time. A comparatively simple mound could acquire stone facing, carved railings, gateways and sculptural decoration. Not every early or regional stupa had all these elements in the same form.

How a stupa was approached and venerated

The central mound of a typical stupa is solid. Worshippers do not enter it as they would enter a prayer hall. Instead, they approach the monument through a gateway and walk around it along the pradakshinapatha.

The customary direction is clockwise, so the stupa remains on the devotee's right side. This is an essential distinction between the stupa as the sacred object of circumambulation and a chaitya hall, which is an architectural space entered by worshippers and may contain a stupa.

Construction materials and patronage

Early stupas could be made from earth and brick, later enlarged or faced with stone. Their construction involved preparing the mound, establishing the relic deposit, constructing supporting elements and adding railings or gateways.

Patronage could come from rulers, merchants, craft guilds and individual devotees. Inscriptions on monument components are particularly valuable because they identify some donors directly. The architecture therefore reflects both religious purpose and the organisation of labour and resources.

Important stupa sites

Sanchi and Bharhut in Madhya Pradesh, Sarnath in Uttar Pradesh and Amaravati in Andhra Pradesh are major sites for understanding the development of Buddhist stupas. Their architectural and sculptural details vary according to date and region.

Prelims focus

  • Anda is the hemispherical mound of a stupa.
  • Harmika is the small railing-like structure above the dome.
  • Yashti supports the chhatra.
  • Vedika is the railing; torana is the gateway.
  • Pradakshinapatha is the path for clockwise circumambulation.
  • Trap: A stupa is not the same architectural form as the hall that may contain one.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 95–97; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, pp. 122–123; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapters 3–4, pp. 21–29 and 46–47.]

pictures.caption: The main architectural parts of a developed Buddhist stupa.

title: Buddhist Stupas: Relic Worship, Architectural Parts and Circumambulation

body:
The Great Stupa at Sanchi

Sanchi is in Madhya Pradesh, near Bhopal. Its monuments include stupas, pillars, temples and monastic remains. The best-known monument is Stupa 1, the Great Stupa.

The earliest brick core of the Great Stupa is generally associated with the reign of Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. During later periods, the monument was enlarged and developed with stone facing, railings, gateways and sculptural decoration. It must therefore be understood as a monument shaped over several centuries rather than as a single unchanged construction.

Architectural features of Sanchi Stupa 1

Sanchi Stupa 1 has a large hemispherical mound, a harmika with the mast-and-umbrella arrangement above it, and a surrounding vedika. Its ceremonial toranas face the 4 principal directions. The monument also includes a lower circumambulatory path and an elevated path reached by stairs.

The gateways consist of upright supports and horizontal crossbars decorated with narrative reliefs. Episodes from the Buddha's life, Jataka stories and auspicious motifs appear in the carvings.

Sanchi Stupa 2 and Stupa 3 are also important. Relic caskets from Stupa 3 are associated with Sariputta and Mahamoggallana, prominent disciples of the Buddha.

Who paid for Buddhist monuments?

Stupas were not funded exclusively by emperors. Inscriptions at Sanchi and other sites record gifts from rulers, merchants, householders, craftworkers, monks, nuns and other devotees. Some inscriptions identify a donor's occupation or home town.

A particularly useful example is the guild of ivory workers, which contributed to a gateway at Sanchi. This shows that a religious monument could be the result of collective donations and specialised craftsmanship, even when its earliest construction had royal support.

Bharhut and Amaravati

Bharhut, also in Madhya Pradesh, is noted for its carved stone railings and narrative reliefs associated with early Buddhist art. These reliefs help identify important stories and symbols used in the decoration of sacred monuments.

Amaravati, in present-day Andhra Pradesh, developed a large and elaborately decorated Buddhist stupa. The monument is especially associated with relief-covered stone slabs and representations of Buddhist narratives. Its sculptural remains are now distributed among several museums.

Why Sanchi survived more fully than Amaravati

In the 19th century, parts of the Amaravati stupa were removed and transported elsewhere. Walter Elliot collected sculptural panels in 1854, and other pieces were dispersed to different collections. The removal of architectural pieces reduced the survival of the original monument in its setting.

At Sanchi, proposals were also made to remove gateways for display abroad, but the original structures remained at the site. The rulers of Bhopal, especially Shahjehan Begum and Sultan Jehan Begum, supported preservation. The Archaeological Survey of India subsequently played a major role in conserving the complex.

The difference illustrates the importance of in situ preservation: retaining an object or structure in its original archaeological location, where its relationship with the rest of the site can still be understood.

Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1989. This was its confirmed status at the content cutoff of 23 November 2026.

Prelims focus

  • Sanchi is in Madhya Pradesh; Amaravati is in Andhra Pradesh.
  • The earliest brick core of Sanchi Stupa 1 is associated with Ashoka.
  • Sanchi Stupa 1 has 4 monumental gateways.
  • An ivory-workers' guild contributed to a Sanchi gateway.
  • The Begums of Bhopal helped preserve Sanchi.
  • Trap: The surviving Sanchi gateway sculptures were not all made during Ashoka's reign.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 82–83 and 95–101; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, pp. 27–34 and 46–47; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi, Description and Inscription details, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Visitors and stoneworkers at an early historic Buddhist stupa complex.

pictures.alt: Sanchi’s gateways stayed at their original site; Amaravati’s sculptural panels were removed and dispersed among museums.

title: Sanchi, Bharhut and Amaravati: Monumental Stupas, Donors and Preservation

body:
What is iconography?

Iconography is the identification and interpretation of images through their subjects, symbols and characteristic attributes. In Buddhist architecture, sculptures on stupas, gateways, pillars and cave walls may communicate events from the Buddha's life, episodes from earlier births and qualities associated with revered figures.

Identifying a sculpture requires attention to its setting and associated symbols. A wheel, tree or empty seat may have a specific meaning within a Buddhist narrative rather than simply representing an everyday object.

Early symbolic representations of the Buddha

Many early Buddhist reliefs represented the Buddha's presence or important events without depicting him directly in human form. This convention is often called aniconic representation.

SymbolCommon associationExplanation
Bodhi treeEnlightenmentAssociated with the Buddha's enlightenment at Bodh Gaya
Empty throne or seatBuddha's presence or meditationIndicates a revered presence without a human figure
Dharma wheelFirst sermonAssociated with teaching at Sarnath
StupaMahaparinirvanaMay evoke the Buddha's final passing and veneration
FootprintsBuddha's presence or pathSymbolise the revered teacher without depicting his body

The meaning of a symbol depends on context. For example, an ordinary wheel in an unrelated scene should not automatically be identified as the Buddha's first sermon.

Human representations of the Buddha

From approximately the 1st century CE onward, major centres such as Mathura and Gandhara developed influential sculptural traditions showing the Buddha in human form. This development did not mean that all symbolic representations disappeared.

  • Mathura: Located in present-day Uttar Pradesh, this centre drew upon established local sculptural traditions, including large Yaksha figures. Early Buddha images often display a strong body, broad shoulders and an upright or seated posture.
  • Gandhara: Associated with the northwestern region of the subcontinent, this tradition combined local artistic practices with features influenced by Hellenistic and other regional traditions. Wavy hair, deeply modelled drapery and carefully shaped facial features are familiar characteristics.
  • Sarnath: Gupta-period images often show a refined, slender Buddha with smoothly treated surfaces and garments that appear closely attached to the body. A famous seated Buddha from Sarnath is associated with the teaching of the dharma.

Mudras and the identification of figures

A mudra is a meaningful hand gesture used in an image. In Buddha sculpture, gestures can help identify the subject:

  • Abhaya mudra: Raised hand with palm facing outward, associated with reassurance or fearlessness.
  • Dhyana mudra: Hands arranged in the lap, associated with meditation.
  • Dharmachakra mudra: Gesture associated with teaching or turning the wheel of dharma.
  • Bhumisparsha mudra: Hand directed towards the earth, associated with calling the earth to witness enlightenment.

Recognisable marks such as the ushnisha, a raised cranial feature or hair arrangement, can also assist identification. The overall context remains important because gestures and visual conventions developed over time.

Bodhisattvas and narrative reliefs

A Bodhisattva is a being associated with the path to enlightenment. In Mahayana Buddhist traditions, Bodhisattvas are particularly associated with compassion and assistance to others.

Padmapani is recognised through the lotus, while Vajrapani is associated with the vajra or thunderbolt. Both figures appear in Buddhist visual traditions, including the famous paintings at Ajanta.

Jataka stories narrate earlier births of the Buddha and frequently appear as sculptural scenes on stupas or painted scenes in caves. At Sanchi, the Vessantara Jataka is among the narratives represented. The presence of a narrative scene should be distinguished from a single devotional image.

Prelims focus

  • The Bodhi tree is associated with enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.
  • The dharma wheel is associated with the first sermon at Sarnath.
  • Mathura and Gandhara were major centres for early Buddha images.
  • Abhaya mudra represents reassurance; dharmachakra mudra is associated with teaching.
  • Padmapani is associated with the lotus; Vajrapani with the vajra.
  • Trap: Early symbolic representations and later human images of the Buddha are not mutually exclusive artistic traditions.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 99–104; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, pp. 26–31 and 48–55.]

pictures.alt: Five Buddhist symbols matched to their common meanings, with the lotus identifying Padmapani and the vajra identifying Vajrapani.
pictures.caption: Major Buddhist symbols and the events or meanings associated with them.

title: Buddhist Sculpture and Iconography: Recognising Symbols and Buddha Images
